metadata.title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering

problem.statement: The paper addresses the challenge of improving passage retrieval in open-domain question answering, where traditional sparse vector space models are the de facto method and dense retrieval methods have not consistently outperformed them without complex pretraining.
limitations_of_prior_work: Traditional sparse vector space models like TF-IDF or BM25 struggle to retrieve contexts with semantic matches (synonyms or paraphrases) that lack lexical overlap.
ORQA (Lee et al., 2019)'s Inverse Cloze Task (ICT) pretraining is computationally intensive, and it is unclear if regular sentences are good surrogates for questions in the objective function.
ORQA (Lee et al., 2019)'s context encoder is not fine-tuned using pairs of questions and answers, potentially leading to suboptimal representations.

method.name: Dense Passage Retriever (DPR)
method.key_idea: The embedding is optimized for maximizing inner products of the question and relevant passage vectors, with an objective comparing all pairs of questions and passages in a batch, using a simple dual-encoder framework without additional pretraining.

components.name: Passage Encoder (E_P)
components.function: Maps any text passage to a d-dimensional real-valued vector.

components.name: Question Encoder (E_Q)
components.function: Maps the input question to a d-dimensional vector.

components.name: FAISS
components.function: An extremely efficient, open-source library for similarity search and clustering of dense vectors, used to index all M passages offline for efficient retrieval.

techniques.name: Dot Product Similarity
techniques.purpose: To define the similarity between the question and the passage vectors.

techniques.name: Negative Log Likelihood Loss
techniques.purpose: To optimize the encoders such that relevant pairs have higher similarity than irrelevant ones.
techniques.details: Maximizes the log likelihood of the positive passage among positive and negative passages in a batch.

techniques.name: In-batch negatives
techniques.purpose: To efficiently reuse computation and increase the number of training examples.
techniques.details: For a batch of B questions and their relevant passages, any (q_i, p_j) pair is a positive example when i = j, and negative otherwise, effectively creating B-1 negative passages for each question.

techniques.name: BM25 negative passages
techniques.purpose: To provide 'hard' negative examples during training.
techniques.details: One additional BM25 negative passage (top passages returned by BM25 that don't contain the answer but match most question tokens) is added per question.

techniques.name: BERT (base, uncased)
techniques.purpose: To implement the question and passage encoders.
techniques.details: Two independent BERT networks are used, and the representation at the [CLS] token is taken as the output vector, with d = 768.

methodology.architecture: Dual-encoder framework using two independent BERT (base, uncased) networks.
methodology.training_objective: Negative log likelihood of the positive passage, optimizing for maximizing inner products of question and relevant passage vectors.
methodology.training_data: Pairs of questions and passages from Natural Questions (79,168 questions), TriviaQA (78,785 questions), WebQuestions (3,417 questions), CuratedTREC (1,353 questions), and SQuAD v1.1 (78,713 questions), using a Wikipedia dump (Dec. 20, 2018) pre-processed into 21,015,324 passages of 100 words.
methodology.compute_requirements: Computing dense embeddings for 21 million passages takes approximately 8.8 hours on 8 GPUs. Building the FAISS index on 21 million vectors takes 8.5 hours on a single server. Reader training was done on eight 32GB GPUs.
methodology.inference_cost: DPR processes 995.0 questions per second, returning top 100 passages per question, on an Intel Xeon CPU E5-2698 v4 @ 2.20GHz with 512GB memory using FAISS. BM25/Lucene processes 23.7 questions per second per CPU thread. Reader inference latency is around 20ms for the single passage case.

settings: Multi (DPR trained using combined datasets excluding SQuAD)
In-batch negative training with batch size 128
One additional BM25 negative passage per question
Trained for up to 40 epochs for large datasets and 100 epochs for small datasets
Learning rate of 10^-5 using Adam, linear scheduling with warm-up, and dropout rate 0.1
Reader considers up to 100 retrieved passages
Reader samples one positive and 23 negative passages from top 100 retrieved passages (m=24)
Reader training batch size of 16 for large datasets and 4 for small datasets

main_findings.claim: DPR outperforms Lucene-BM25 in top-20 passage retrieval accuracy on Natural Questions.
DPR outperforms Lucene-BM25 in top-20 passage retrieval accuracy on TriviaQA.
DPR outperforms Lucene-BM25 in top-20 passage retrieval accuracy on WebQuestions.
DPR outperforms Lucene-BM25 in top-20 passage retrieval accuracy on CuratedTREC.
DPR outperforms BM25 in Top-5 accuracy on Natural Questions.
main_findings.setting: in-batch negative training with 1 BM25 negative

main_findings.claim: DPR establishes new state-of-the-art on Natural Questions for end-to-end QA.
DPR achieves state-of-the-art on TriviaQA for end-to-end QA.
DPR (Multi) achieves state-of-the-art on WebQuestions for end-to-end QA.
BM25+DPR (Multi) achieves state-of-the-art on CuratedTREC for end-to-end QA.
DPR trained with only 1,000 examples outperforms BM25.

ablation_insights.delta: +6.0% Top-20 accuracy (69.1% vs 63.1% on NQ dev for Gold 7 negatives)

ablation_insights.effect: Accuracy consistently improves as batch size grows.
ablation_insights.delta: +3.9% Top-20 accuracy (73.0% for batch size 128 vs 69.1% for batch size 8 on NQ dev)

ablation_insights.effect: Adding a single BM25 negative passage substantially improves results.
ablation_insights.delta: +5.0% Top-20 accuracy (78.0% vs 73.0% on NQ dev for 1 BM25 negative)

ablation_insights.component: Number of additional BM25 negative passages
ablation_insights.effect: Adding two BM25 negatives does not help further compared to one.
ablation_insights.delta: -0.9% Top-20 accuracy (76.4% vs 77.3% on NQ dev for 2 vs 1 BM25 negatives with 31 gold negatives)

ablation_insights.effect: Has only a small impact on retrieval accuracy.
ablation_insights.delta: -1.0% Top-k accuracy (77.1% vs 78.1% Top-20 on NQ dev)

ablation_insights.effect: L2 performs comparably to dot product, and both are superior to cosine.
ablation_insights.delta: -2.0% Top-20 accuracy (76.1% for L2 NLL vs 78.1% for DP NLL on NQ dev)

ablation_insights.component: Loss function (Triplet Loss vs Negative Log Likelihood)
ablation_insights.effect: Using triplet loss does not affect the results much.
ablation_insights.delta: -0.9% Top-20 accuracy (77.2% for DP Triplet vs 78.1% for DP NLL on NQ dev)

ablation_insights.component: Cross-dataset generalization (DPR trained on NQ applied to WQ/TREC)
ablation_insights.effect: Generalizes well, with some performance loss but still greatly outperforms BM25.
ablation_insights.delta: -3 to -5 points Top-20 retrieval accuracy (69.9% vs 75.0% for WQ, 86.3% vs 89.1% for TREC)

efficiency_results.latency: around 20ms per query (for reader, single passage case)
efficiency_results.throughput: 995.0 questions per second (for DPR retrieval of top 100 passages)
efficiency_results.comparison: DPR retrieval is incredibly efficient (995.0 questions/second) compared to BM25/Lucene (23.7 questions/second per CPU thread).

contributions.description: Demonstrated that simply fine-tuning question and passage encoders on existing question-passage pairs is sufficient to greatly outperform BM25, suggesting additional pretraining may not be needed.
Verified that a higher retrieval precision translates to a higher end-to-end QA accuracy in open-domain question answering.
Proposed Dense Passage Retriever (DPR), a simple and effective dense retrieval model that achieves new state-of-the-art results on multiple open-domain QA benchmarks.

comparisons.difference: ORQA uses a sophisticated inverse cloze task (ICT) objective for additional pretraining and does not fine-tune the context encoder with question-answer pairs, while DPR trains both encoders using only question-passage pairs without additional pretraining.
comparisons.evidence: DPR achieves 41.5% EM on NQ, outperforming ORQA's 33.3% EM.

comparisons.difference: REALM includes additional pretraining tasks and employs an expensive end-to-end training regime with asynchronous passage encoder tuning, whereas DPR does not rely on additional pretraining or complex joint training schemes.
comparisons.evidence: DPR achieves 41.5% EM on NQ, outperforming REALM News's 40.4% EM.

comparisons.difference: BM25 is a sparse, term-matching method sensitive to keywords, while DPR uses dense, learned representations that capture lexical variations and semantic relationships.
comparisons.evidence: DPR outperforms BM25 by 9%-19% absolute in Top-20 passage retrieval accuracy (e.g., 78.4% vs 59.1% on NQ).

comparisons.other_method: Joint training of retriever and reader (following ORQA)
comparisons.difference: The paper's approach trains the retriever and reader in isolation, while the compared method jointly trains them with a fixed passage encoder and backpropagation to the question encoder from a combined loss.
comparisons.evidence: Joint training obtains 39.8% EM on NQ dev, which is lower than DPR's 41.5% EM with pipeline training.

limitations: DPR shows lower performance on SQuAD due to high lexical overlap between passages and questions (giving BM25 an advantage) and a biased training distribution from only 500+ Wikipedia articles.
Building an index for dense vectors is computationally intensive and time-consuming (8.8 hours for embeddings, 8.5 hours for FAISS index for 21M passages) compared to Lucene's 30 minutes.
DPR might lack sufficient capacity to represent salient phrases which appear rarely, as shown in qualitative examples where BM25 performs better.

key_terms.definition: A task that answers factoid questions using a large collection of documents.
A component that first selects a small subset of passages where some of them contain the answer to the question.
A machine reader that can thoroughly examine the retrieved contexts and identify the correct answer.
Models like TF-IDF or BM25, which match keywords efficiently with an inverted index and represent questions and contexts in high-dimensional, sparse vectors.
Representations complementary to sparse methods, capable of mapping synonyms or paraphrases to vectors close to each other even without exact token matching.
A system that uses a dense encoder (E_P) to map any text passage to a d-dimensional real-valued vector and builds an index for all passages for efficient retrieval.

A training strategy where computation is reused to effectively train on B^2 (q_i, p_j) question/passage pairs in each batch, with (q_i, p_j) being a positive example when i = j and negative otherwise.
